# Precision cylinder boring (`boring_machine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by water_wheel, sand_loam_casting, gears_gear_trains, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A cast cylinder is never round or straight inside, and a piston cannot seal in it. To correct it, a cutter head must travel along a path fixed by the machine, not by the rough hole. A stiff iron bar passes right through the cylinder and turns in bearings at both ends; the cutter head slides along the bar, fed by a rack or screw, while the cylinder is clamped still without being squeezed out of shape. Earlier mills, with the cutter on the end of an overhung bar resting on a shoe inside the bore, followed every error of the casting. Wilkinson's large engine bores let Watt seal full-size pistons without excessive friction or steam leakage. Inspect the diameter at several depths and orientations: a bore can have the right diameter at its mouth and still be tapered or oval further in.
- Pitfalls:
  - A cutter guided by the hole it is cutting: it copies the error
  - A bar supported at one end only, which sags and chatters
  - Clamping a thin cylinder tightly; it springs back oval when released
  - Thinking a Newcomen engine needs this; it managed with hand-scoured bores and a water seal, Watt's commercial engines benefited from much closer fits
- History: europe: 1540 – Biringuccio shows water-powered reaming of cored cannon; 1713–1740s Jean Maritz bores cannon from the solid, vertically then horizontally; c. 1770 Smeaton's cylinder boring mill at Carron; 1774 John Wilkinson's cannon-boring patent; 1775 his cylinder boring mill at Bersham, used for Boulton and Watt's engines; china: none known before the 19th c.; bronze and iron guns were cast with a cored bore
- Read:
  - L. T. C. Rolt, Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools (1965)
  - H. W. Dickinson & Rhys Jenkins, James Watt and the Steam Engine (1927)
